lead: A 2D cartoon and a 3D game character look different because they are made by different techniques, not because of different software. 2D animation draws flat pictures or slides separate parts around; 3D animation builds a model, gives it a skeleton, and moves the skeleton. The technique fixes what the tool must do: a sprite editor, a rig editor or a particle engine. This chapter covers the four 2D techniques, the six-stage 3D pipeline, the two ways to pose a skeleton, and the four ways to drive motion.
prereq: You need Unit 2 for composite transforms (rotating a limb about its joint) and Unit 3 for polygon meshes, lighting and rendering.

sections.h3: 2D techniques: drawn frames and moved parts

blocks.text: Frame-by-frame animation, also called cel animation, draws every frame by hand. A cel is a transparent sheet: the moving character is painted on the cel and the background is painted once underneath, so only the character is redrawn. At 24 frames per second (fps), one second of film needs 24 drawings. That is why studios draw only key poses and let the software or an assistant fill the rest (see 5.2).
Rotoscoping traces live footage. The animator projects the film frame by frame and draws over each frame. Motion comes out human because it was filmed, but the cost is still one drawing per frame.

Sprite animation stores the moving object once as a small bitmap and stamps it at a new position on a fixed background each frame. Memory holds one sprite plus one background, not 240 full frames, which is why sprites suit games. Moving the sprite is a pure translation (Unit 2).

Cut-out animation, which some syllabi call puppet animation, builds the character from separate parts: head, upper arm, forearm. Each part sits on its own layer with its own transform. Moving a part means changing its rotation or position; nothing is redrawn. Hinging two parts at a shared point is the 2D version of a skeleton.
A 3D shot cannot start until the model exists. The stages run in a fixed order, and each stage hands a file to the next.

items: Modelling: build the polygon mesh of vertices, edges and faces (Unit 3).
Texturing: wrap images and material values on the surface to set colour, roughness and pattern.
Rigging: build a skeleton of bones inside the mesh and bind each vertex to a bone with a weight.
Animation: pose the rig at chosen frames and set the timing.
Lighting: place lights and cameras for the shot (Unit 3).
Rendering: compute the final 2D image for every frame. At 24 fps that is 24 renders for each second of film.

blocks.text: Rigging is the stage 2D does not have. A bone is a segment with a pivot. A vertex weighted 1.0 to a bone follows it exactly; a vertex weighted 0.5 between two bones moves halfway. Those weights are why a shoulder bends smoothly instead of tearing open.

Tool families follow the stages, not the brand: polygon modellers and sculpting tools for modelling; image and procedural texture tools for texturing; rig editors for skeletons; animation timelines with curve editors; renderers; and compositors that combine renders with live plates.
A rig is a chain: shoulder to elbow to wrist. Each joint carries an angle, and kinematics is the arithmetic that turns those angles into a hand position.
x = L₁ cos θ₁ + L₂ cos(θ₁ + θ₂),   y = L₁ sin θ₁ + L₂ sin(θ₁ + θ₂)
blocks.where: x, y are the hand position in metres measured from the shoulder; L₁ and L₂ are the upper-arm and forearm lengths in metres; θ₁ is the shoulder angle from the horizontal in radians; θ₂ is the elbow angle relative to the upper arm in radians.

blocks.text: Forward kinematics (FK) walks outward from the root: set θ₁ and θ₂, then compute the hand. The arithmetic is direct and gives exactly one answer, but landing the hand on a cup means guessing angles by trial.

Inverse kinematics (IK) walks inward from the hand: the animator drags the wrist to a target and the solver finds θ₁ and θ₂ backwards. The answer is not unique, because the elbow can point up or down, so IK needs constraints such as a joint limit or a pole vector. Use FK for waving, tails and free arcs; use IK for a foot planted on the ground or a hand gripping a rail.

sections.h3: Four ways to drive the motion

items: Keyframe: the animator sets poses at chosen frames and the software interpolates every property between them (see 5.2).

Procedural: a rule or formula sets the value on every frame. A bobbing float is h = A sin(2πft); a flag flap is a wave travelling along the cloth. No poses are stored, only the formula and its parameters. Some syllabi call this expression-driven animation.

Motion capture: a performer wears reflective markers or a sensor suit, cameras record marker positions in 3D many times per second, and software maps that data onto the rig. It captures subtle human motion fast but needs cleanup and a matching skeleton.

Particle systems: fire, smoke, rain and sparks. Each particle is a point with position, velocity, lifetime and size. Every frame the system applies forces such as gravity and wind, updates velocity and position, spawns new particles and kills old ones, then draws each as a sprite or a small mesh. The animator sets the rules, not the frames.

blocks.text: A 3D animation that never touches motion capture is still 3D animation. The rig with keyframes is the normal case; mocap is one input method among four.

figure.caption: A 10 s cel clip at 24 fps is 240 frames. With a key pose every 6 frames, each group of six is 1 key and 5 in-betweens, so the clip needs 40 keys and 200 in-betweens.

examples.question: A 2D cel animation runs for 10 s at 24 fps. The animator draws one key pose every 6 frames. Find the total number of frames, the number of key poses and the number of in-between frames.
steps: Frames: N = fps × time = 24 frames/s × 10 s = 240 frames.
Key poses: one pose every 6 frames, so K = 240 ÷ 6 = 40 key poses.
In-betweens: the frames that are not key poses, B = N − K = 240 − 40 = 200 in-between frames.
Check: 40 key poses + 200 in-betweens = 240 frames, which matches the total.
examples.answer: The clip has 240 frames, 40 key poses and 200 in-between frames.
examples.check:
fps = 24
dur = 10
step = 6
frames = fps * dur
keys = frames // step
inb = frames - keys
print(frames)
print(keys)
print(inb)

examples.question: A flag is animated procedurally with height h = A sin(2πft). Take A = 0.4 m and f = 0.5 Hz. Find h at t = 0.5 s and state how many frames that is at 25 fps.
steps: Frames: 0.5 s × 25 frames/s = 12.5 frames, that is frame 12 or 13 depending on rounding.
examples.answer: At t = 0.5 s the flag height is 0.4 m, which falls at frame 12 or 13 of a 25 fps clip.
examples.check:
import math
A = 0.4
f = 0.5
t = 0.5
h = A * math.sin(2 * math.pi * f * t)
print(round(h, 4))
print(0.5 * 25)

traps: Swapping forward and inverse kinematics. 'Rotate the shoulder and see where the hand lands' is FK; 'put the hand here and let the software bend the elbow' is IK.
Assuming every 3D animation needs motion capture. A hand-keyed rig on a timeline is ordinary 3D animation; mocap is only one input method.
Counting in-betweens wrongly. The key poses are part of the total, so B = N − K; do not add one, and do not count in-betweens as the total.
Calling cut-out animation 3D because the parts sit on separate layers. If every transform applied is 2D, the output is 2D.
Jumbling the pipeline order. Rigging comes after the model and before animation, and rendering is always last and always done per frame.

quiz.a: A transparent sheet on which one frame of the moving character is painted. It is laid over a background painted once, so the background is not redrawn.

quiz.q: List the six stages of the 3D pipeline in order.
quiz.a: Modelling, texturing, rigging, animation, lighting, rendering.

quiz.q: Why does sprite animation use far less memory than frame-by-frame animation?
quiz.a: It stores one small bitmap of the moving object plus one background, and moves the bitmap by translation. Frame-by-frame stores a full frame for every frame of the clip.

quiz.q: A clip runs 5 s at 30 fps with a key pose every 10 frames. Find the frames, key poses and in-betweens.
An animator wants the character's hand to stay on a table edge while the torso moves. Should the rig use FK or IK? Why?
quiz.a: IK, because the hand position is the fixed target and the solver computes the shoulder and elbow angles backwards. With FK the hand would drift and the animator would have to re-guess angles on every frame.

quiz.q: Give one clear difference between rotoscoping and motion capture.
quiz.a: Rotoscoping traces 2D images of live footage frame by frame into drawings. Motion capture records 3D positions of markers on a performer and drives a 3D rig with that data.

quiz.q: Why is a particle system better than a keyframed mesh for rain?
quiz.a: Rain has thousands of independent drops. Keyframing each is impossible, but particles are spawned by a rule, moved by gravity and wind, and killed after a lifetime. The animator sets density, speed and wind once and the whole shower follows.

quiz.q: A flag height follows h = A sin(2πft) with A = 0.4 m and f = 0.5 Hz. Find h at t = 0.5 s.

beyond: Not for the exam. In a studio the pipeline is split across people and files: a modeller, a rigger, an animator, a lighter and a compositor touch the same asset, and shot files reference the asset instead of copying it. Real-time engines now render 3D scenes at interactive rates, so game animation leans on blended clips and state machines rather than one long timeline. Machine learning is used for motion capture cleanup and for guessing in-between poses. Search 'skeletal animation skinning', 'inverse kinematics solver FABRIK' and 'particle system smoke simulation' to go further.
